questions.q: Identify the specific action Gandhi takes immediately after being served the official notice to quit Champaran, and state what this action reveals about his attitude toward British authority.
questions.a: Gandhi signs the receipt for the notice but writes on it that he will disobey the order. This reveals he respects legal procedure (signing) but refuses to legitimize unjust authority (disobeying), embodying his principle of non-violent non-cooperation. A wrong answer (e.g., "he tore up the notice" or "he left immediately") shows the student confuses Gandhi's civil disobedience with either rebellion or submission, missing the precise calibrated resistance that defines satyagraha.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Gandhi refuses Charles Freer Andrews' offer to stay and help in Champaran, and what this reveals about his concept of leadership.
questions.a: Gandhi refuses because accepting help from an Englishman would imply the cause depends on white patronage, undermining the self-reliance he wants to instill in Indians. This reveals his leadership is not about winning a single battle but about building a people's capacity to stand alone. A wrong answer (e.g., "Gandhi was proud" or "he didn't like Andrews") shows the student reads the incident personally rather than as a deliberate pedagogical act to model self-reliance.

questions.q: APPLY: The text states Gandhi "chided the lawyers for collecting big fee from the sharecroppers" and said "law courts are useless" for the fear-stricken peasants. Using this evidence, write a PEEL paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) analyzing Gandhi's view on the relationship between legal justice and psychological liberation.
questions.a: Point: Gandhi prioritizes freedom from fear over legal justice for the oppressed. Evidence: He tells lawyers, "Where the peasants are so crushed and fear-stricken, law courts are useless. The real relief for them is to be free from fear." Explanation: He recognizes that colonial courts, designed by the oppressor, cannot deliver justice to those terrified of the system; true justice requires first dismantling internalized fear. Link: This belief drives his entire Champaran strategy — mass civil disobedience is not just a legal tactic but a psychological liberation tool. A weak answer would merely quote the line without explaining WHY courts fail the fear-stricken or HOW civil disobedience cures fear.

questions.q: ANALYZE: Compare Gandhi's negotiation strategy with the planters' representative (demanding 50%, accepting 25%) with a conventional lawyer's approach. What does the difference reveal about his goal?
questions.a: A conventional lawyer would maximize monetary compensation (aim for 100% refund). Gandhi demands only 50%, then accepts 25%, because his goal is not money but breaking the planters' "prestige" and proving peasants have rights. The planters' surrender of ANY money shatters their aura of invincibility. A wrong answer focusing on the "low settlement" misses that Gandhi explicitly states "the amount of the refund was less important than the fact that the landlords had been obliged to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige."

questions.q: EVALUATE: The text says Gandhi's politics were "intertwined with the practical, day-to-day problems of the millions" and "not a loyalty to abstractions." Critique this statement using two specific examples from the chapter where Gandhi addresses non-political issues (sanitation, education, health) during the Champaran struggle.
questions.a: Example 1: Gandhi opens primary schools in six villages and brings teachers (Mahadev Desai, Narhari Parikh, their wives, Devadas, Kasturbai) because he sees "cultural and social backwardness." Example 2: He addresses health by getting a doctor to volunteer, distributing castor oil, quinine, sulphur ointment, and tackles sanitation by asking Kasturbai to teach cleanliness and writing to the ashram to dig new latrine trenches. These prove he treats political freedom as inseparable from human dignity in daily life. A weak answer would list the activities without connecting them to the "loyalty to living human beings" philosophy.

questions.q: CREATE: Write a 50-word diary entry from Gandhi's perspective on the night before his court appearance in Motihari, capturing his "conflict of duties" and the reasoning behind his decision to disobey.
questions.a: "Tonight I weigh two duties: not to break the law as a public example, and to serve the peasants who have no voice. The law commands me to leave; conscience commands me to stay. I will sign the receipt, but write my disobedience. Not defiance — obedience to a higher law. The peasants' fear must end." A poor answer would sound like a modern protestor ("I'll fight them!") rather than Gandhi's precise, conscience-driven, non-violent reasoning.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the protagonist involves examining the central character's traits, motivations, decisions, and development through their actions, speech, thoughts, ______, and the author's narration, to understand their role in advancing the theme and narrative structure of the text.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a lawyer preparing a case: your "client" is Gandhi, and the "______" is the text of "Indigo." You don't just list adjectives — you prove each trait with a specific incident.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to write a structured 150-200 word character sketch of Gandhi in "Indigo" using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) with at least three distinct textual evidences, and explain how his character embodies the principles of satyagraha and self-reliance as depicted in the chapter.
